title: Fields white for harvest (John 4:27–42)
hook: she leaves her water jar and tells the town; many believe

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Samaritan woman at the well at noon, and a conversation that crossed an old divide. Your line was in spirit and in truth. Where did you find God without a building? Day six hundred three.

Just as Jesus tells her who he is, the disciples come back with lunch. John says they marveled that he was talking with a woman, and nobody dared ask him why. Picture the scene. Twelve men holding bread, standing awkwardly. And the woman doesn't wait for anyone to explain. She turns and walks fast back toward town. And she leaves something behind, sitting by the well. The one thing she came for. The text says it in one quiet line: "The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city."

Why mention the jar? John wastes very few words. A water jar was heavy and valuable, and the whole reason for her trip. Leaving it says she's in a hurry, and maybe that she'll be back. Many readers also hear something more: she came for ordinary water and found what Jesus called living water, so the old jar can wait. In town, her message is simple, almost funny: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Not a sermon. An invitation, and a question. Come and see, the same words Philip used with Nathanael a few days before. Meanwhile, back at the well, the disciples are pushing food at Jesus. Master, eat. And he says, "I have meat to eat that ye know not of." Meat, in old English, just means food. They wonder if someone brought him a sandwich. He explains: his food is to do the will of the one who sent him. Then he points at the fields. "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest." Some readers picture the townspeople at that very moment, streaming out across the fields toward the well, maybe in light-colored clothes. The text doesn't say so, but the timing fits. Ripe grain in that country turns pale gold, nearly white. The ending is the best part. Many Samaritans believe because of her word. Then Jesus stays two days, and more believe, and they tell her: "Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves." She brought them; they met him themselves. And they call him the Savior of the world.

Here's the practice: leave something behind in your hurry to share. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good that happened to you lately. A kindness, a book, a moment that opened something. Who would want to hear about it? Picture their face. Then think of your water jar: the small thing that usually stops you sharing. Being busy. Worrying it'll sound strange. Let it sit by the well for a minute. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to say come and see. If you don't, just rest with the person you pictured. The bell holds the time.
Fields white for harvest. Jesus's words as the Samaritan town comes out to meet him: the harvest isn't months away, it's already here.
Your line: she left her water jar. Today, tell one person about something good, and let one small task wait while you do. Day six hundred three.

howItsDone: Christians often read this passage when talking about sharing their faith; many hear in the woman's "come, see" a model of simply inviting someone rather than arguing.

fork.setup: you're the woman. you've just heard the stranger say who he is, and his friends are staring at you. what do you do?

leave the jar and run to tell the town.

fork.reveal: she leaves her waterpot and goes into the city: "come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did."

original.note: Greek: white, bright. The fields are already pale, ready to cut.

trapdoor: what you thought: a detail about a forgotten water jar.
what it means: she came for water and left in a hurry to share what she'd found, and the town came out to meet him.
what a scholar hears: her words echo "come and see" from chapter one, and the Samaritans end by calling Jesus the Savior of the world, a title found only here in the Gospels.

λευκαί (John 4:35) feminine plural of λευκός; confirm form and pronunciation.
